analysis.investment_thesis: Fiem Industries is a high-quality auto-ancillary compounder with exceptional capital efficiency (~40% ROIC) and a near-debt-free balance sheet, but at a ~5.7% earnings yield the Magic Formula finds it priced for perfection — too expensive to generate formula-grade returns. Hold if owned; wait for a better entry below INR 1,600.
key_strengths: Exceptional ROIC ~40% (EBIT INR 322 Cr / Invested Capital ~INR 804 Cr) — top-decile capital efficiency in auto ancillaries
Aggressive deleveraging: finance costs collapsed from INR 16 Cr (2016) to INR 2 Cr (2025), freeing earnings power and compounding equity at 15.3% net profit CAGR
Dominant OEM supplier with sticky customer relationships; 54.5% promoter holding signals owner-operated discipline
key_risks: Earnings yield too low at ~5.7% (EBIT INR 322 Cr / EV ~INR 5,670 Cr) — Magic Formula requires >12%; leaves thin margin of safety
Capex surging from INR 19 Cr (2022) to INR 130 Cr (2025), compressing FCF to INR 132 Cr despite record profits — capital intensity rising
Auto sector cyclicality: FY2020–21 revenue/profit decline showed vulnerability to industry downturns and two-wheeler demand slumps
red_flags: FCF conversion deteriorating: FCF/Net Profit fell from ~213% (FY2020) to ~64% (FY2025) as capex accelerates — watch if this persists
Borrowings jumped from INR 23 Cr to INR 62 Cr in FY2025 despite strong cash generation — new capex cycle may pressure the pristine balance sheet
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Running the Magic Formula on Fiem gives a split verdict. On quality, it scores brilliantly: EBIT/Invested Capital (EBIT INR 322 Cr ÷ (Equity INR 1,080 Cr + Debt INR 22 Cr − Cash INR 298 Cr) ≈ INR 804 Cr) implies ~40% ROIC, well above the 25% "excellent" threshold, corroborated by the reported ROCE of 27.8%. The business earns exceptional returns on every rupee deployed, with operating margins expanding from 12.8% (2016) to 13.3% (2025). On cheapness, however, EV ≈ INR 5,670 Cr versus EBIT of INR 322 Cr yields only a 5.7% earnings yield — barely half the 12% minimum the formula targets. At current prices, the market is already pricing in the quality.

The capex ramp (INR 130 Cr in FY2025 vs. INR 19 Cr in FY2022) is the key swing factor: if the new capacity drives a step-change in revenue and EBIT, the earnings yield problem partially self-corrects over 2–3 years; if demand disappoints (as in FY2020–21), the now-rising debt and FCF compression become a real concern. The business itself is among the better-run mid-cap auto ancillaries in India — but at a P/E of 24.7x and P/B of 5.5x, Greenblatt's formula says "good business, wrong price." A 30–35% correction to ~INR 1,500–1,600 would push earnings yield above 8–9% and make this a compelling formula buy.
